newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark marks royal jubilee with pomp and pride.
newsitem.headline: Denmark marks royal jubilee with pomp and pride.

text.p: The winter sun shone, drums rolled and crowds cheered as Queen Margrethe II of Denmark rode in a gilded state coach through her capital on Wednesday to mark 25 years on the throne.

Flag-waving admirers, young and old, watched as the monarch passed through the city streets, escorted by a troop of the Royal Horse Guards in uniforms of blue, scarlet and gold, with drawn sabres and plumed helmets gleaming.
"She waved, she waved at me!" an excited toddler shouted to his kindergarden teacher.
"That's an experience the kids don't get if they just watch it on television," the teacher said.

Along the route from Amelienborg Palace to Copenhagen City Hall brass bands played -- mostly marches, although a fife and drum band in period dress surprised listeners at one point by launching into the theme from "The Flintstones" cartoon series.
Margrethe became queen on January 14, 1972, but as the date also marks the death of her father, King Frederik IX, Tuesday's public events were relatively restrained.
Under a grey sky she attended family memorial prayers and an official thanksgiving service and later hosted a state banquet where her mother, Queen Ingrid, 86 seemed to allude to her own mortality.

In an unscheduled address which brought tears to the eyes of many dinner guests, the old queen spoke to her eldest daughter -- using her family nickname of "Daisy" -- recalling her birth in April 1940, one week after Germany occupied Denmark.

"I recall, many years ago, when you entered the world, your father's and my first child. The times were very grave, very difficult and very bleak but you appeared like a tiny ray of sunshine and meant everything to father and me," she said.
"Daisy, you have two wonderful sons, so I am confident that I can safely close my eyes and they will do their best for Denmark. God bless Denmark."
But on Wednesday the sun broke through and the previous day's sombre atmosphere turned to merrymaking.

The red and white Danish flag hung from every city steeple, from buses and from shopfronts and it was a broadly smiling queen who reviewed honour guards of the Danish army, navy and air force in the city's main square.
Also taking part were 40 men of the Britain's Princess of Wales' Royal Regiment, of which Queen Margrethe is allied colonel-in-chief.

It is the first royal jubilee since 1937, when Margrethe's grandfather, King Christian X, celebrated his quarter-century as ruler. His son Frederik, who succeeded on Christian's death in April 1947 was only three months short of his own jubilee when he died after a two-week illness.

Public celebration in the capital peaks on Wednesday evening with a gala performance of the Royal Ballet and a firework display. On Saturday the royal family visits Denmark's second city, Aarhus, for more parades and jubilee visits are planned later in the year to the Danish North Atlantic territories of Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
